WeaveTogether Guide

How to read the app and weave from it: the notation that shows one strip at a time, the settings that order the crossings and cut the strips, and the patterns a lattice can be woven in.

Pipeline

TryTriWeave ends with a lattice. WeaveTogether starts there: the lattice becomes a weave, the weave gets a plan, and the plan is shown to the hands. A pattern acts between lattice and weave; the material, the profile and the number of weavers act on the plan.

What is planned

Three decisions: the order in which the crossings are made, where every strand is cut into strips and how the strips are joined, and which strip the hands move at each crossing.

What the weaver sees

One strip at a time: where it runs, what it passes over and under, and the cell it closes. The same plan twice, as a model in space and as a line of time.

What a pattern changes

Only the weave. Whatever the pattern, what comes out has strands, a crossing per lattice edge and a ring of crossings round every cell, so the planners read it without knowing the pattern.

In the app, from top to bottom

1 File: a lattice from TryTriWeave, or a built-in one. 2 Discretization: material, start, method, weavers, profile. 3 Pattern. 4 Markers. 5 Lengths. Then follow the History bar with the piece in your hands.

What you need on the table

Strips cut to the lengths the plan lists (5 Lengths), clips for the crossings that do not hold yet, and tape or coloured clips if you want to mark strips or cells (4 Markers).

Three live views of the app

At the end of each part the app itself runs inside this page, set to that part's example: the notation, the plan, the patterns.

Notation

Where it comes from, how its marks work, and what they are on the 3-D canvas, in the History bar and as markers.

Where the notation comes from

The notation was put together from instruction systems that already work with few words — origami diagrams, building instructions, road signs, the history bar of a CAD program — and then corrected each time the screen and the hands disagreed. The table gives every source, what it does well and what was taken from it.

SourceWhat it does wellWhat WeaveTogether took from it
Origami diagrams (Yoshizawa–Randlett; Rozenberg 2019)A small closed key of symbols learned before step 1; one drawing per state; arrows for the action; dashed for what is hidden.One strip per state. The arrow is the action. Where the strip goes under, its marks go under with it.
Road and rail signage of Kinneir and CalvertOne arrow shape in two weights, read at a glance when much else is going on.current (bold arrow), passed (what is behind it), path (thin line): three marks, one shape.
LEGO as a graph (Kollsker 2020, ch. 2)A construction as a graph: bricks are nodes, connections are edges; connectivity as a quick test of whether it holds.Cells are nodes, crossings are edges. A crossing whose strips do not hold yet is a clip point. Later the whole planning graph.
Build order by taking apart (LEGO patent US 8,374,829; ORIZU, Akitaya et al. 2013)Disassemble on the computer, then reverse: no loose piece, stay near the last piece.Rings from a start, close a cell early, stay beside the last cell.
Beady (Igarashi, Igarashi, Mitani 2012)Every new bead is locked by finished faces; the wire in use is coloured; next and previous.The strip in hand in a vivid colour, everything else calm; step by step; the strip's length shown.

One strip at a time

A weave is learned through the strip in the hand. Every state of the notation shows exactly one strip to move: where it runs, how far it has come, and what it passes over and under. Everything else steps back.

Three states of a strip

Vivid: the strip in hand. Light: woven before. Grey: in the weave but not woven there yet — the remainder. In the app it hangs straight off its last crossing; here it is drawn along the line it will take.

Three marks on the strip in hand

Path, a thin centre line: where this strip runs. Passed, a thick bar: what this step has threaded so far. Current, an arrow whose tip stops just before the crossing being made, so the crossing itself stays visible.

Over and under, said three times

By colour: the strip on top covers the other at the crossing. By word: the tag under the view. By the marks: line, bar and arrow lie on the strip and go under with it.

The band

Of the other strips, only what the strip in hand crosses in this step is vivid: 1.5 lattice edges of it, centred on the crossing. A crossing of the cell that this strip does not touch stays light, and nothing is vivid before it is woven.

A crossing between two strips already in hand

Neither strip is being threaded, so neither gets the arrow: a dot sits on the crossing, and the tag names both strips — S8 under S3.

Names and badges

S7 is strand 7; S7.2 its second strip after the cut. The cell being built carries its number in the order on a dark disc, hollow once it is closed. A cell with other than six sides shows its number of sides.

Over

The strip in hand lies on top: its colour, its bar and its arrow run across the crossing unbroken. The strip it crosses gets its band, and disappears under it for the width of the strip.

Under

The crossed strip lies on top, band and all, and the marks of the strip in hand pass beneath it: line, bar and arrow are cut where the strip is covered, exactly as the strip is.

Reading a step at the table

  • Find the vivid strip: it is the one in your hand.
  • Follow the bar to the arrow: that is how far you are.
  • Read the tag that is filled: over or under.
  • Check the crossing: whichever strip covers the other in the picture covers it on the table.

Two lengths

The band is 1.5 lattice edges long (BAND). A crossing section of a fifth of a segment on either side of a crossing (CROSS_SEC = 0.2) is laid and coloured as soon as that crossing is made, so the weave grows crossing by crossing, not segment by segment.

u_x: the place of the crossing along the crossed strip; a: the lattice edge.

On the 3-D canvas

The canvas shows the piece as it lies on the table: the woven part on the surface, the strips in hand hanging off it, and one cell being built. Each thing drawn is a layer that can be switched off.

Colour of the laths

By piece (default) · by family · by weaver · by part of the figure · by stress · by marker. The woven part is 10 % less saturated than its hue, so the strip in hand stands out.

The remainder

Hanging: straight off its outermost woven crossing, as long as what is left (default). Or on the surface along its future path. Or hidden.

The camera

Fixed · follows by sliding · follows by turning to the cell. The turn is yaw and pitch only: test users lost the match between piece and model once the view rolled.

Which side is up

Over and under are read from outside the surface. Flip the lath side swaps the laths and the words together. Top of the model turns files whose up axis is not Z.

Clip points

A strip holds itself by friction once it is woven through a few crossings (holds after, ). Until both strips of a crossing hold, the crossing carries a ring: put a clip there.

The path of the order

A line from cell to cell in the order they are closed: solid behind, dashed ahead. It shows at a glance where the work goes next and where it jumps.

In the History bar

The History bar is the same plan as a line of time: a chip for every strip, a tag for every crossing. It plays, steps and scrubs like the history of a CAD model.

Two rows, two grains

History moves by step: one strip through one cell. Weave direction moves inside a step: one crossing at a time. All sub-steps (the default) plays every crossing of every step.

What a step is

Cell tour: per cell, first the strip in hand that makes the most crossings there is carried on, then each new strip is added, and the last of them closes the cell. Ring to ring: a run — the crossings one weaver makes in a row with one strip in hand.

The words on the tags

over · under for the strip in hand; end where it ends at the rim; between for a centre strip of the hemp leaf; both names — S8 under S3 — for a crossing between two strips already in hand.

A joint, crossing by crossing

The overlap of a joint is woven like anything else, so each of its crossings is a tag: over or under, in a second colour, with “overlap 2 of 4” in its tooltip.

The weave read as a surface

χ = cells − crossings + closed triangles of the woven part. A step that closes a loop carries a small ring on its chip: solid for a loop round the shape, dotted for a loop round a patch still to weave.

Keys

← → step · ↑ ↓ crossing · space play · R reverse · Home, End.

Markers

A weaver holds a real, half-woven piece and looks at a model on a screen. A marker ties the two together: a clip or a bit of tape on a strip or at a cell of the piece, and the same strip or cell in the same colour on the model.

What can be marked

A strip, or the opening of a cell. Each mark has a colour, a name of your own and a check box; a second click on the model takes it off.

How a mark is kept

A strip mark is one crossing of its strand, not a strip number. When the plan is cut differently, the mark stays on whichever strip holds that crossing: mark a strip, then switch the length above. Marks are saved per file, in the browser.

The switch

In the header of 4 Markers, after the count. On: the laths are coloured by marker and the marked cells are ringed. Off: the colouring from before returns.

The colours

Okabe and Ito's eight, told apart with any colour vision and close to the tapes and clips at hand.

Not to be confused with

The History bar's rollback marker (), which marks a moment, not a place.

Try it · the notation in the app

The app itself, on the flat patch. Step with the History bar at the bottom; orbit with the mouse; switch layers under Display.

B

Discretisation

The algorithm, its theory and method; the weave profile, one parameter at a time; and how several weavers are planned.

The weave is a graph

The lattice TryTriWeave hands over is a triangulation of the surface. The weave is its medial graph: one crossing in the middle of every lattice edge, and strips that run straight on from crossing to crossing. To discretise a weave is to choose an order on that graph and to cut its strands into strips a person can handle.

The objects

  • Cell — an opening of the weave; a vertex, V. Singular when it has other than six sides.
  • Crossing — two strips, one over; an edge, E.
  • Triangle — the small opening between three strips; a face, F.
  • Strand — a strip before it is cut: a walk straight on. Strip — a piece of a strand no longer than the material. Joint — two strips of one strand overlapping by k crossings.

What a plan is

The order of the crossings, each made once. The cut of every strand into strips, with their joints. And the hands: at each crossing, which of the two strips is moved.

The rules of a real weave

  • A strip is woven on from where it is threaded, never at two places with the middle free.
  • A strand is continued only through crossings that are already made.
  • A strip in the weave hangs out of it until it is done.
  • A cell holds only when all its crossings are made.

Why it is planned, not searched

There are E! orders: 208! for the small tube. Both planners construct one order greedily; an optimiser then moves a handful of parameters ().

2 for a closed shape like a sphere, 1 for a disc, 0 for a tube or a torus. Used for the whole lattice and, crossing by crossing, for the part woven so far.

The material: strips, cuts and joints

A strand of the lattice can be metres long; the material is not. The cut belongs to the plan: where a strip starts, how far it runs, and how the next one is joined to it. Three numbers describe the material, and one rule keeps every strip in one woven piece.

Three numbers for the material

Length limit, in centimetres: the longest strip the material gives. Joint overlap k, 0 to 4 crossings. Holds after N crossings: a strip woven through fewer is held by a clip, so a crossing is a clip point until both its strips hold.

One woven part per strip

A strip is threaded where the order first needs its strand and is woven on from there. Where the order returns to a strand further away than follow (), a new strip starts there and the two are joined where they meet.

The joint is woven

The strip that is there first is the lower layer; the end of the later one lies on it and passes the crossing strips as it does. Each overlap crossing is a tag of its own in the History bar: “over S7 · overlap 2/4 on S4.1”.

Choosing the length

Set the scale in 1 File, type the longest strip you can cut, then press Suggest length: it lists the lengths at which the number of strips drops and marks the shortest one with the fewest strips and every joint at its full overlap.

Cutting list

5 Lengths charts every strand before the cut and every strip after it, in centimetres. Cut before you weave: a strip is never lengthened, only joined.

Where the cut is decided

In the planner, after the order: every strand is cut where the tour came back to it from further than follow, and wherever a piece would exceed the length limit (cutByTimes). Suggest length re-plans at each length from half to twice the limit (lengthSteps).

(7)The fewest strips a length allows
Nmin⁡=∑smax⁡ ⁣(1,  ⌈LsLmax⁡⌉)N_{\min} = \sum_{s} \max\!\Bigl(1,\; \Bigl\lceil \frac{L_s}{L_{\max}} \Bigr\rceil \Bigr)Nmin​=s∑​max(1,⌈Lmax​Ls​​⌉)

L_s: the length of strand s; L_max: the length limit. Every strip more than this is a joint more.

algorithms.js · minStrips

Two planners

Two algorithms construct the order. The cell tour thinks in cells and is the app's default. Ring to ring thinks in crossings and weighs every move. Both are greedy; neither searches the orders. Each has a handful of parameters of its own, shown here one diagram at a time.

The cell tour

How it goes

  • A start rule picks a cell.
  • Breadth-first search numbers every cell by its ring: how many cells it is away from the start.
  • One step weaves the fan of a cell: the crossings on its ring and the one opposite each side.
  • Inside a cell: carry on the strip in hand, add the new strips, close.
  • Ring after ring, always beside the last cell.

Parameter · start

Most reachable: the cell from which half of the singular cells are soonest reached. Centre: the smallest sum of distances to them. Flattest: the regular cell farthest from any of them. Rim: the lowest cell of the boundary — and round that rim first where it is the end of a tube. Auto plans all four and keeps the one that fits the profile best. Switch the rule above: the rings, the order and the fit change.

What was added for real shapes

A limb once begun is finished (); a hole the weave has closed round is patched first; a tube end goes round its rim first; a torus starts from the shortest loop round it and is woven one way round.

Cell tour planner.js

start ← start rule, or a cell picked on the surface
ring[v] ← breadth-first distance from the start
          (tube end: from the whole rim · torus: one way
           round from a loop)
while a cell is not woven:
  where ← a limb that is begun, else a hole the weave has
          closed round, else anywhere
  r     ← the lowest ring with an unwoven cell in `where`
  cell  ← on the front, in ring r, not waiting for a strip:
          beside the last cell → most woven neighbours
          → nearest
  weave the fan of `cell`
cut every strand where the tour came back to it from
  further than `follow`; join the parts

follow · 0 to 8 lattice edges, default 4

The tour reaches a cell that needs a strand already in the weave. If that strand is woven up to closer than follow, its strip is woven on to the cell first. Further away, a new strip starts at the cell and the two are joined where they meet. Larger: fewer strips and joints, longer ways for the hands.

strip length · 0.5 to 1 of the material

The length a strip is cut to, as a share of the length limit — for both planners. Shorter strips leave shorter remainders, so fewer loose ends lie in the way, at the price of more strips and joints.

finish first · limbs and holes, or rings only

A limb — a part that sticks out and ends: an ear, a branch up to its rim — is woven to its end as soon as the tour reaches it, and a hole is woven before the tour goes on. With rings only everything is left to the rings from the start, and a limb can stand open for most of the weave.

Ring to ring

How it goes

  • The seed is the lowest rim; every crossing gets a level: how many rings it is away from it.
  • The front is the unmade crossings beside the woven part; the weaver's side is the stretch of it within reach.
  • Every candidate on the lowest ring of the side gets a cost — a sum over about twenty rules in seven groups. The cheapest is made.
  • A strip is cut when it is threaded, and woven from there without gaps; a joint is made first.

When to choose it

Ring to ring follows how people weave a tube or a branch: once round, then the next ring. It moves the hands less than the cell tour on long shapes, and several weavers are planned with it (). The cell tour is easier to follow cell by cell on small pieces.

Ring to ring sequence.js

seed ← the lowest rim (closed shape: the lower end of its
       longest axis; with a handle: the shortest loop round
       it) unless most strands would turn back from there
level[e] ← hops from the seed
while a crossing is not made:
  front ← unmade crossings beside the woven part, in pieces
          where a rim, a hole or a branch divides it
  side  ← this piece of the front within `side` (4 a)
  C     ← a crossing left behind within reach, else the
          lowest ring of the side, else the side, else
          the piece, else another piece
  make argmin over C of Σ weight × term
  a new strip is cut as it is threaded; a joint is made first

Seven factors · ¼ to 4, default 1

Each factor scales one group of rule weights: stay in the area, keep the strip, few new strips, close cells, curved parts first, hold the singular cells, ring order. A factor above 1 makes its group count more in every decision.

side · 2 to 10 lattice edges, default 4

How far along the front the weaver's side reaches. A narrow side keeps the hands in one place; a wide one lets the weaver take the cheapest crossing further along the ring.

strip length · 0.5 to 1 of the material

As for the cell tour ().

You rarely set these by hand

Pick a profile () and press Tune: it tries a few hundred settings and keeps the plan that fits the profile best. The table under the radar lists the values it found.

The weave profile

A plan is not good or bad; it is good for someone. The profile is seven things a weaver can ask of a plan. Each is measured on the finished plan and scored from 0 to 1, and each has a weight that says how much it matters. The weighted mean of the scores is the fit.

Fit

The weighted mean of the seven scores. Move a weight: nothing about the plans changes, only what matters, and another plan may come out on top.

fit = Σ wi si / Σ wi

Five profiles to start from

balanced · stay where the work is · fewest joints · figure first · clear way. Or set the weights yourself.

(9)Fit and objective
fit=∑iwi si∑iwi,f=1−fit  +  [incomplete]  +  0.002 g\mathrm{fit} = \frac{\sum_i w_i\, s_i}{\sum_i w_i}, \qquad f = 1 - \mathrm{fit} \;+\; [\text{incomplete}] \;+\; 0.002\, gfit=∑i​wi​∑i​wi​si​​,f=1−fit+[incomplete]+0.002g

The optimiser brings f down. A plan that is not complete is pushed out by 1; g counts strips woven at two places with the middle free.

profile.js · objective

The seven axes, each defined and then shown on a real plan

the real plan

no jumps

A jump is a move the hands should not have to make: the next crossing lies further away than one strip of the material is long, measured along the weave, or it lies on another front — another stretch of the open edge of the weave, more than three lattice edges away. Anything shorter is a move.

1 / (1 + jumps per 100 crossings)

Drag the next crossing away from the last one. Inside the ruler it is a move; past it, or on another front, it is a jump.

short moves

Each time the next crossing is not a neighbour of the last one, the hands move. The way is the sum of those moves along the weave, in lattice edges a. A step to a neighbouring crossing costs nothing.

1 / (1 + way per crossing / 0.2 a)

Click crossings in the order you would make them. Every move that is not to a neighbour leaves a line, and the lines add up.

few joints

The strips of the plan against the fewest the length limit allows, every strand in as few strips as its length needs. Every strip more is a joint more. The score is relative to the limit: it says how well the plan uses the material it is given.

fewest strips / strips

The eight strands of the capped cylinder as bars. Move the limit: the cuts the length forces, and beside them the strips the plan really has.

clear way

How many loose ends lie in the way. The end being threaded sweeps a fan: half a lattice edge to either side near the crossing, a quarter of the distance further out. Counted are the hanging remainders of strips already in the weave that enter it. Nothing has to be held — the material lies on the table and is taken strip by strip — this counts what has to be pushed aside.

1 / (1 + in the way per crossing / 2)

Drag the tip of the blue end, the one with the arrow; drag the grey ends; shorten the strip. The figure scores one crossing; the axis is the mean over all crossings, counted for whichever of the two strips at a crossing has fewer in its way.

few closing strips

A closing strip is joined to other strips at both of its ends: it has to fit between two woven parts, and both ends go into a joint. A strip with one free end is simply woven on.

1 / (1 + 3 · closing strips / strips)

One strip between two woven parts. Switch each of its ends between free and joined, and set how many strips of a plan are closing.

figure first

The recognisable parts early and in one go, the mean of three shares. Curvature early: Σ|K| of the closed cells, averaged over the sequence. Features early: tips, saddles and bends — singular cells at most two lattice edges apart — each by how soon it is complete with the cells round it. Limbs in one go: for a part that sticks out and ends, how little of the rest is woven while it stands open.

mean of the three shares (two on a shape without limbs)

Drag the marks along the sequence: when each singular cell closes, when the feature is complete, when the limb is begun and finished.

shape held

The mean of up to three parts; one that does not apply to the shape is left out. Loose weight: the share of the spring-back energy — bending and twist of the strips, from the geometry — that sits in segments whose cell is still open. Hold: how long a closed singular cell waits for the crossings round it. Wrap-around: on a tube or a handle, how early the first loop round the shape closes; until then the weave is a sheet.

mean of 1 − 2 · loose share, 1 / (1 + (hold − 1) / 4), 1 − t / T

Three sliders, three part scores, one mean. Untick a part that the shape does not have.

What Tune moves

Dual annealing

Generalised simulated annealing as in SciPy's dual_annealing, without its local search, because a plan is not a smooth function of its parameters. A heavy-tailed visiting distribution (qv = 2.62) that narrows as the temperature falls, a generalised Metropolis acceptance (qa = −5), a chain of 2 · dim plans per temperature — all parameters at once for the first half, then one at a time — and a restart near the best at 2 % of the start temperature.

What it gives, said plainly

On the benchmark set with 120 plans (measured on 12 November): ring to ring gains 2.7 points of fit on average and 9.8 at most, the cell tour 2.0 and 6.9 at most — about what as many random parameter sets give at that budget, as in the run shown. Tuned parameters hardly carry over: those tuned on the tube (+9.8 there) give +0.7 on the tree, +0.5 on the bunny and +0.9 on the capped cylinder.

The budget

60 to 240 plans, as many as fit in a minute on the lattice in the view. The best plan is kept only if it beats the default parameters.

i: the chain's number. The typical step at T_0 = 1 is a third of a parameter's range.

Several weavers

A large object is woven by several people at once. The rule for it is short: multiplayer is not multitasking. Every weaver has a front of their own and works next to their own work; where two fronts meet there is a seam.

As built: ring to ring

  • 1 to 6 weavers; a start each — a rim each from the lowest, then the cells farthest from the starts taken, or the cells picked as A, B, C.
  • Rounds: one crossing per weaver per round.
  • A weaver's candidates are only the crossings that share a cell with one it has made.
  • Where fronts meet, strands are cut and joined: the seam. A strip one weaver carries on from another is a hand-over. A weaver whose front the others have closed waits.

As built: the cell tour

Every cell belongs to the nearest start. Each weaver tours its own cells ring by ring; they take one cell each in turn. Nothing is balanced: it is the baseline.

Setting it up

2 Discretization → method: ring to ring → weavers: 2 or more. Pick start… and click a cell for A, then for B. The History bar gets a lane per weaver (); each of you follows your own letter.

Tried and dropped

  • Areas by distance from the starts: every weaver spirals, as one would alone.
  • One shared front: the same path as one weaver's, dealt out at random.
  • The cheapest crossing anywhere on the ring: a weaver ends up on the far side of the others — multitasking.

What comes next: the proposal, not built

  • Even work: Σ (1 + |K|) over a weaver's crossings.
  • A map first: the parts where the rings split and merge, and their order — a travelling-salesman question.
  • Two behaviours to choose from: parts first, or free but never across another's woven part.
  • The seam by rule: a remainder within the overlap is woven into the other's lattice; a longer one is handed over, no cut.
  • Weavers start apart and grow towards each other.

What it costs today

On the tube, two weavers need 47 strips and 25 joints where one needs 33 and 11; three need 52 and 30. Tree, three weavers: every weaver one area, 360 joints, 487 rounds. The joints where areas meet head-on are the price.

Related work: games on graphs

The multi-start graph can be read as a game: a cell taken is a binary state, but joints and overlaps are how a weave continues, so the planning involves coalitions and non-zero-sum dynamics. Multiplayer games on regular graphs (Wang, Perc & Szolnoki 2024), coevolutionary games (Perc & Szolnoki 2010) and interdependent networks (Parshani, Buldyrev & Havlin 2010; Wang, Szolnoki & Perc 2013) study such dynamics. The planner here is cooperative — one cost for the whole weave, and the payoff is completion — and none of that work is in the code.

Pattern

Five weaves on one lattice, explained on the flat patch, on the cone with a five-sided tip and on the cone with a four-sided tip.

A pattern is a rule on the same lattice

A pattern does not need a planner of its own. It turns the lattice into a weave of the same kind — strands, a crossing on every lattice edge, a ring of crossings round every cell — by one of three moves, so everything in parts A and B still applies.

Move 1 · rule

The same strips, another over and under. The strips grow wide and lie in three layers. Star in rounds.

Move 2 · lattice

A finer lattice is derived — a new cell in every triangle — and woven by its own rule. Mad weave.

Move 3 · guests

Strips the lattice does not have are added: beside the strands (star weave) or through the middle of the cells (hemp leaf). The planners never see them; they come into the finished plan ().

Five patterns: the rule, how it is woven, the 5 and the 4

The flat patch shows the rule. One wedge taken out gives a five-sided tip, two wedges a four-sided one: there the surface closes into a cone, the three families of strips stop being three, and each pattern has to say what it does at the tip. Every figure is the app's own weave and plan, drawn flat from above.

Hexagonal weave六角孔編 · 六つ目編みliùjiǎo kǒng biān · mutsume-ami — “hexagonal-hole weave”, “six-eye weave”

1 · the rule

One strip through every crossing of the lattice, over and under in turn, 0.20 a wide. Every cell is an open hole with as many sides as the cell. This is the weave the lattice is drawn for; every other pattern is made from it.

2 · how it is woven

By the plan of part B, cell by cell or ring to ring: 24 strips and 43 steps on the flat patch. Each strip reads over · under · over … along its length.

3 · at the 5 and at the 4

The hole has five or four sides, and the strips round it lie on each other in turn exactly as round a six-sided one. Away from the tip nothing changes; but the three families of strips are no longer three — follow one strip round the tip and it comes back in another direction.

Star weave蛛網編 · 星紋編zhūwǎng biān · xīngwén biān — “spider-web weave”, “star-pattern weave”

1 · the rule

Every strand in several strips lying against each other — a band on every side of a hole, and the hole stays open. Where two bands cross, every strip of one crosses every strip of the other. At the corners of a centre the strips nest as a V, the strip nearer the hole on top; elsewhere a block is woven as one crossing.

2 · how it is woven

Band by band from the centre: round the centre the strip nearest the hole on every side, then the second on every side, then the third — 6, 12, 18 on the flat patch — and from there outward one band after the other. The strips are named in that order: S1 … S6, S1b … S6b, S1c … S6c.

3 · at the 5 and at the 4

The centre is the singular cell: 5, 10, 15 strips round a pentagon — three strips on every side of a five-sided hole, as in a rattan ball — and 4, 8, 12 round the four-sided cell. A band is as wide as fits everywhere on the lattice: 0.088 a and 0.087 a a strip.

Star in rounds蛛網編 · wide stripsthe star read as rounds

1 · the rule

The same strands as the hexagonal weave, one strip each, but 0.70 a wide: wide enough to close on each other, three layers deep. Read as rounds round a cell, as a spider builds its web: round 1 is the ring of the hexagonal weave round the centre, and every further round lies outside the last and is pushed under the strips that already cross its place.

2 · how it is woven

By the plan of part B, started at the centre: 24 strips, 43 steps and four rounds to the rim on the flat patch. All 132 crossings follow the rule of the rounds; in 18 triangles the three strips go round, each over the next, and have no stack.

3 · at the 5 and at the 4

The rounds are counted from the singular cell: four rounds to the rim on both cones, 110 of 110 and 88 of 88 crossings by the rule. Five wide strips close round the five-sided hole, four round the four-sided one.

Hemp leaf麻葉編 · 麻の葉編みmáyè biān · asanoha-ami — “hemp-leaf weave”

1 · the rule

The hexagonal weave, its strips 0.15 a wide, with a centre strip along every line of the lattice. Three centre strips cross in the middle of every six-sided cell (the 米), and at every crossing of the hexagonal weave the centre strip lies between its two strips.

2 · how it is woven

Threaded afterwards: the hexagonal weave is made first, then every centre strip is pushed along its line, between the two strips of each crossing — a step of its own for every strip, its tags reading between. 21 centre strips and 64 steps on the flat patch. Or laid in as you weave ().

3 · at the 5 and at the 4

In a cell of five sides a centre strip cannot go straight on: the five lines end there, and the cell stays open. In the four-sided cell the lines do go straight on: two centre strips cross in its middle, a cross where a six-sided cell has a 米.

Mad weave亀甲編 · anyam gilakikkō-ami — “tortoise-shell weave”; Malay anyam gila, “mad weave”

1 · the rule

Three layers of strips and no holes. Every strip is a 2-1 twill with the strips of both other directions — over two and under one against one of them, under two and over one against the other — and what shows is a tiling of rhombi. It is woven on a finer lattice — a new cell in every triangle, the √3 lattice — with strips 0.46 a wide and three times the crossings.

2 · how it is woven

By the plan of part B on the finer lattice: 48 strands and 159 steps on the flat patch. Along a strip the tags read over · over · over · under · under · under: over two and under one against one direction, under two and over one against the other.

3 · at the 5 and at the 4

Every cell of the lattice becomes a star point: six rhombi round a six-sided cell, five at the five, four at the four. Every triangle becomes a cube corner. The cones have 51 and 41 star points, 80 and 64 cube corners.

Patterns in the plan

The planners plan the lattice's own weave. What a pattern adds is brought into the finished plan afterwards: cut to the length limit, joined, named, and given steps of its own. That keeps one planner for all patterns. Two patterns let the weaver choose how their strips come in.

Band by band, or pass by pass

Band by band (the default) weaves the star from its centre, every strip a step of its own and no hexagonal weave first. Pass by pass makes the whole hexagonal weave first — the middle strip of every band, cell by cell as the method plans it — then a second strip for every band, then a third.

Threaded afterwards, or laid in

Threaded afterwards: one step per centre strip after the hexagonal weave; its tags read between. Laid in as you weave: no extra steps; the tag of a crossing that holds a centre strip carries a bar, and the strip's name where it is picked up. Which one depends on the material.

What the History bar says

A strip of the mad weave reads over · over · over · under · under · under. A centre strip reads between · between. A strip beside a strand reads over and under against the strips already there.

How a pattern's strips enter the plan

They become strands of an extended weave that the view, the History bar, the length charts and the exports read (extendWeave, augmentPlan). The planners, the topology and the scores keep to the lattice's own weave.

Limits

  • The profile's scores and Suggest length count only the lattice's own weave, not the strips a pattern adds.
  • The star from its centre is an order for one weaver, and the profile does not score it; with several centres everything is counted from the centre the weave starts at.
  • The star's width is the one that fits everywhere; where lattice edges are short the bands are narrower than they could be. The lattice is not yet made for the band.
  • Hemp leaf: afterwards means after the whole hexagonal weave, not as soon as the crossings along a strip's line are made.
  • Mad weave: at strips of 0.46 a there is a crossing every 0.29 a; the pattern wants a larger lattice edge, and the handedness of the reference is not confirmed.
  • A strip is drawn at its final height even where the strip it will step over is not woven yet.

Limits of the drawing

  • Where the surface turns sharply the strips of a band are drawn as one stiff band; what a band should do there — fan out, overlap, a finer lattice — is open.
  • On a very coarse lattice a joint inside a band is drawn badly.
  • A quad mesh is cut along arbitrary diagonals on import, which gives an irregular weave.

The benchmark set

v4 and v5 cone (1 cm per unit, 30 cm strips) · two tubes (0.3 cm, 50 and 45 cm) · two Y shapes (90 and 100 cm) · two capped cylinders (155 and 100 cm) · the tree with three branches (100 cm). Overlap 4, holds after 3.

What people changed

A first trial by colleagues: gaps between the lath segments; after it the laths became splines and the marks moved onto the strip. Test users: a camera that rolls loses the match with the piece. Reading the bunny's plan: the ears were left open, which led to finish first.

What is missing

Someone following a plan from the first strip to the last: time, mistakes, where they stop. And a woven object beside its plan.

Limits and open questions

The planners are described as they are. These points are open; the limits of the patterns are listed in .

  1. A hold rule for the cell tour. After a singular cell closes, the cells round it should come next. Ring to ring rewards exactly those crossings; the cell tour has no such rule, and hold is its weak point on shapes with many singular cells (bunny ×7.3 against ×5.1, tree ×7.7 against ×4.3).
  2. Finish first inside Tune's search. With clear way at 1 and figure first at 0.2, Tune switches it off and the bunny's ears stand open again. It may belong to the weaver as a switch only.
  3. The weight of figure first in the profile clear way: 0.1 now; 0.5 would keep the limbs closed.
  4. What the best length is. Suggest length marks the shortest length with the fewest strips and every joint at its full overlap. The least waste, or the most even strips, are other readings.
  5. The order of the parts of a shape is the planner's; the weaver cannot choose it yet.
  6. Several weavers. What is built gives every weaver a front; even work, a map of parts and a seam without a cut are proposed and not built ().
  7. Tune. At 120 plans dual annealing gains about what random parameter sets gain, and parameters tuned on one lattice gain less than a point on another ().
  8. Shape held is geometry only. The spring-back energy is read from the bending and twist the surface asks of a strip; nothing is simulated.
  9. The notation is for the screen. A printed key, tapes on the strips and a poster are outside this page.
  10. No study with people yet ().

  • Loop, C. (1987). Smooth Subdivision Surfaces Based on Triangles. MSc thesis, University of Utah. to confirm
    The smooth surface under the star's bands.

Optimisation and topology

  • Tsallis, C. & Stariolo, D. (1996). Generalized simulated annealing. Physica A 233, 395–406. · Xiang, Y., Sun, D., Fan, W., Gong, X. (1997). Phys. Lett. A 233, 216–220. to confirm
    Generalised simulated annealing, the scheme behind dual annealing; used here without the local search of SciPy's dual_annealing.
  • Tree–cotree decomposition (for example Eppstein 2003, Dynamic generators of topologically embedded graphs). to confirm
    How the loops round a shape are labelled before weaving.
  • Ester, M., Kriegel, H.-P., Sander, J., Xu, X. (1996). DBSCAN. to confirm
    Considered for cutting a front into pieces.

    Related work for several weavers.
  • Wang, Z. et al. (2013). Interdependent network reciprocity in evolutionary games. arXiv:1308.1947.
    Related work for several weavers.
  • Parshani, R., Buldyrev, S., Havlin, S. (2010). Interdependent networks: reducing the coupling strength leads to a change from a first to second order percolation transition. arXiv:1004.3989.
    Related work for several weavers.

Patterns

  • 居有竹. 竹編基礎教學 · 基礎編法: the step sheets 蛛網(轉框) and 麻葉(轉框). to confirm

  • Verrill, H. A. Symmetries of mad weave patterns. J. Math. Arts 20 (2026). to confirm

Glossary

One word per thing, as used on this page. The right column gives the word the app or its code uses where that differs.

WordMeaningIn the app or the code
cellAn opening of the weave; a vertex of the lattice.
singular cellA cell with other than six sides.a 5, a 7 · valence
crossingWhere two strips cross, one over; an edge of the lattice.knot
strandA strip before it is cut: the whole walk through the lattice.
stripA cut piece of a strand, no longer than the material.piece · “by piece”
lathThe solid a strip is drawn as on the 3-D canvas.Display → laths
jointTwo strips of one strand overlapping by k crossings.joint overlap
remainderThe part of a strip in the weave that is not woven yet.loose end · hanging
fanThe crossings a cell makes: on its ring, and the one opposite each side.
ringThe cells at one breadth-first distance from the start. Also: the crossings round one cell (its ring).level (ring to ring)
step, crossing of a stepOne strip through one cell (cell tour) or one run of a strip (ring to ring); one crossing of it.step · sub-step · tick
front, sideThe unmade crossings beside the woven part; the weaver's stretch of it.
move, jumpA change of place to a crossing that is not a neighbour; one longer than a strip or to another front.skip · jump
limb, holeA part that sticks out and ends. A patch the weave has closed round — not a cell's opening.
wrap-around loopA closed band round the shape that cannot be filled: round a tube, a branch, a handle.round
hold, clip pointHow long a closed singular cell waits for the crossings round it. A crossing held only by friction.holds after
bandThe vivid stretch of a crossed strip (notation). The strips of one strand in the star weave (pattern).highlight · ply
guestA strip a pattern adds to the lattice's own.centre strip · strip beside a strand
weaverA person weaving at the same time as others.weavers
profile, axis, fitThe seven weights; one thing a plan is scored on; the weighted mean of the scores.objective = 1 − fit
markerA reference mark on a strip or a cell. Also the History bar's rollback marker.4 Markers
discretisationChoosing the order of the crossings and cutting the strands into strips.2 Discretization
